paper_context.research_question: Can a contextually generated geometric (subspace) representation of individual word vectors be used to identify metaphoric vs. literal uses of adjective-noun pairs, including for unseen phrases (zero-shot)?
main_claims: A contextual geometric method that projects adjective-noun word pairs into ad-hoc subspaces and extracts simple geometric features (triangle side lengths) can identify metaphoric vs. literal usages with performance comparable to or exceeding prior compositional supervised methods on the Gutiérrez et al. (2016) dataset.
The model operates in an effectively zero-shot fashion because it requires only individual word vectors (no phrase vectors) and thus can be applied to unseen adjective-noun pairs.

Contextual selection of subspaces (based on salient PMI co-occurrence dimensions) yields interpretable geometric relationships that correlate with degrees of metaphoricity, supporting a view of metaphor as contextually emergent along a spectrum rather than a strict categorical mapping.
Model performance improves with larger co-occurrence windows and with subspaces that incorporate information from both constituents (adjective and noun).
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Predictive performance on metaphoricity classification (precision, recall, F-score, accuracy) via cross-validation on an established dataset (Gutiérrez et al. 2016).
Comparison against relevant baselines and prior methods (word2vec cosine baseline, Gutiérrez et al. V1/V2 tensor methods, majority-class).
Ablation/parameter sensitivity: effect of subspace selection technique, subspace dimensionality, and co-occurrence window size.
Interpretability of learned representations: analysis of geometric features (e.g., norms, pairwise distances, triangle geometry) and their correlation with metaphoricity.
Generalisability / zero-shot capability: whether the method can be applied to novel/unseen adjective-noun pairs without phrase-level data.
Statistical significance of reported improvements (e.g., significance tests reported in paper).

Section 3: explicit procedural description (PMI calculation, subspace selection, triangle construction).

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: PMI-based word-vectors built from the December 2014 Wikipedia dump (top 200k words, smoothing a=10,000) capture the salient lexical associations needed to characterise metaphoric vs. literal usage.
supporting_evidence: Section 3: 'the model is based on a standard distributional vector space, using pointwise mutual information (PMI) cooccurrence statistics calculated over... December 2014 dump of English language Wikipedia.'
PMI formula and parameter (a=10,000) stated in equation (1).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If Wikipedia PMI vectors do not capture associations relevant to metaphoric usage (e.g., domain-specific metaphors), subspace selection and geometric features may be uninformative, reducing predictive performance and limiting generalisability.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Selecting top-k PMI dimensions (by various criteria) yields contextually meaningful subspaces that reflect relevant semantic associations for the input word pair.
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Section 3 (Method); definitions of Joint, Independent, Zipped, Adjective Only, Noun Only
supporting_evidence: Section 3: description of five selection techniques and rationale that PMI dimensions contain information about a word's most salient associations.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If top-k PMI dimensions are noisy, redundant, or not semantically relevant, the constructed geometry may be arbitrary, degrading interpretability and classifier performance; different selection heuristics might lead to inconsistent results.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Triangle-based geometric features (lengths of AB, AO, BO, CD, etc.) adequately summarise the informative aspects of the subspace geometry with respect to metaphoricity.
supporting_evidence: Section 3: introduction of triangle ABO and CDE features and rationale for expecting correlations with metaphoricity.
Section 4: use of triangle side lengths as input features for logistic regression.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If these summary features omit important geometric information (angles, higher-order relationships, distribution of mass across dimensions), the classifier may miss predictive signals or misattribute importance to certain features (e.g., BO).

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Logistic regression on the selected geometric features is a sufficient classifier to reveal the relationship between geometry and metaphoricity.
supporting_evidence: Section 4: 'We then take the lengths of the sides of the triangles... as features in a logistic regression model, trained to predict the metaphoric/literal label.'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If relationships are non-linear or involve interactions not captured by logistic regression, predictive performance may be suboptimal and analyses (feature importances) may be misleading; alternative classifiers might yield different conclusions.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The Gutiérrez et al. (2016) dataset (8,592 dyads, 23 adjectives) is an appropriate benchmark for evaluating zero-shot metaphoricity detection and for comparing against the prior tensor-based methods.
supporting_evidence: Section 4: description of dataset and its prior use in Gutiérrez et al. (2016).
Background: discussion of Gutiérrez et al. as a prior state-of-the-art method using adjective tensors.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the dataset's construction (adjectives chosen specifically) biases results (e.g., noun-dominant signals), claims about zero-shot generalisability and comparisons to prior work may not hold across broader or more diverse datasets.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The PMI smoothing constant (a=10,000) and choice to use positive-weighted PMI (+1 term) produce stable, meaningful co-occurrence values for building the base space.
supporting_evidence: Equation (1) includes smoothing constant a and +1 term; text notes that values will be positive and 0 indicates no co-occurrence.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Different smoothing or PMI handling (e.g., using PPMI, raw PMI, or SVD-based embeddings) might change the ranking of salient dimensions and thus subspace construction and downstream performance; sensitivity to these choices is not fully characterised.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Vocabulary cutoff at top 200,000 most frequent words is sufficient to cover necessary context dimensions for building informative subspaces.
supporting_evidence: Section 3: 'The top 200,000 most frequent words are taken as the model’s vocabulary... resulting in a very large, very sparse matrix of 200,000 rows representing vocabulary word-vectors.'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Important contextual co-occurrence dimensions may be excluded if relevant words fall outside the top 200k, which could harm subspace quality, especially for less frequent nouns/adjectives or domain-specific metaphors.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Cross-validated F-score reported using shuffled 10-fold cross-validation on the dataset is an adequate estimate of generalisation performance for the method.
supporting_evidence: Section 4: 'we evaluate using standard shuffled 10-fold cross-validation (again following Gutiérrez et al. (2016)). Our evaluation metrics are the standard (micro-)average precision, recall, f-score and accuracy across the 10 folds.'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If folds leak information (e.g., same adjective appears across folds and creates label priors) or dataset imbalance/structure affects shuffle CV, reported F-scores may be optimistic; no held-out unseen-adjective/noun split is reported to test true zero-shot generalisation.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Higher F-scores reported for larger windows and joint subspaces reflect semantic (syntagmatic) signal rather than artefacts of increased dimension or data sparsity.
supporting_evidence: Section 5: interpretation linking window size to semantic vs syntactic signal (reference to Sahlgren (2008)) and observed F-score increases.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If improvements are driven by overfitting due to larger feature sets, or by statistical artefacts of denser co-occurrence counts rather than true semantic signal, the claimed benefit of larger windows or joint subspaces may not generalise.

argument_focus: Contextual subspace selection from PMI word-vectors as a mechanism for capturing metaphoricity.
Use of simple geometric features (triangle side lengths, norms) as interpretable predictors.
Zero-shot applicability by avoiding phrase vectors and relying on individual-word statistics.
Parametric effects: window size, subspace selection technique, and subspace dimensionality on predictive performance.
Interpretive claim that metaphor is a spectrum emergent from contextual geometry.
contribution_targets: Introduce a method for dynamically selecting ad-hoc subspaces per adjective-noun pair using PMI-based word-vectors.
Demonstrate that triangle-based geometric features can be predictive of metaphoricity and used in logistic regression.
Empirically compare performance to Gutiérrez et al. (2016) tensor-based approaches and simple baselines on their dataset.
Provide analyses that link geometric patterns (e.g., BO norm, AB length) to metaphoric vs literal distinctions and a spectrum interpretation.

Re-implement the five subspace selection techniques (Joint, Independent, Zipped, Adjective Only, Noun Only) and verify selected dimensions.
Compute triangle-side features and retrain logistic regression with the same normalization and 10-fold shuffled CV setup; compare reported F-scores and check statistical significance tests.
Verify the claim that noun norm (BO) is the single most predictive feature via single-feature regressions and provide effect sizes, confidence intervals, and stability across folds.
Test zero-shot generalisation: evaluate on adjective-noun pairs containing adjectives or nouns not present in training folds (leave-adjective-out / leave-noun-out splits).
Assess sensitivity to PMI smoothing, vocabulary cutoff, context window sizes beyond tested values, and other embedding alternatives (e.g., word2vec, SVD-PPMI).
Validate significance claims (χ2 tests): report contingency tables, test statistics, degrees of freedom, and exact p-values.
uncertainty_flags: Comparative claims vs Gutiérrez et al. V2 are complicated because V2 was evaluated on a reduced subset (identity unknown); direct comparison may be unreliable.
Statistical testing statements lack details (exact p-values, test statistics).
Zero-shot claim is operationalised as 'no phrase vectors required' but the model is trained on dyads; generalisation to truly novel vocabulary items or domains is not demonstrated.
Table 3 and some analytic numeric results are referenced qualitatively, but full numeric detail (e.g., per-feature F-scores, coefficients) is not reproduced in the text.
Dependence on Wikipedia-based PMI vectors may limit domain generalisation; alternative corpora or methods might yield different subspaces and conclusions.
chaining_notes: Downstream reviewers should first reproduce the PMI base space (exact preprocessing: tokenisation, counting windows, handling of punctuation, vocabulary ranking) because all subsequent subspace selections and claims depend on it.
Validate subspace selection code by comparing dimension indices selected for a sample of adjective-noun pairs to ensure 'Joint/Independent/Zipped' implementations match manuscript descriptions.

When testing predictive claims, include both shuffled CV and leave-one-adjective-out / leave-one-noun-out splits to separate classifier exploitation of adjective priors from genuine geometric signals (this targets A5 and A8).
Request or reconstruct the exact fold/rand seeds if possible to replicate reported CV numbers; if not available, report variance across multiple random seeds.

Probe robustness: vary PMI smoothing a, vocabulary size, and window sizes beyond reported values; compare to dense embeddings (word2vec) to test whether the geometric phenomenon is PMI-specific.
Ask for full tables of logistic regression coefficients, standard errors, and single-feature performance (Table 3) to quantify the asserted dominance of BO and to compute confidence intervals.
Investigate alternative geometric features (angles, cosine distances, higher-order moments) to test assumption A3 that triangle side lengths are sufficient summaries.
If claims about interpretability and spectrum nature are pursued, consider collecting or using graded metaphoricity annotations (rather than binary) to more directly test continuous correlations.

PAPER_CONTEXT: methodological, empirical stance, zero-shot claim, Gutiérrez et al. (2016) dataset comparison
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a contextually generated subspace method: build a large PMI base space from Wikipedia, select per-adjective-noun k-dim subspaces via five heuristics (Joint, Independent, Zipped, Adjective-only, Noun-only), compute simple geometric summaries (triangle side lengths, norms) and use logistic regression to classify metaphoric vs literal adjective-noun pairs. Main empirical claim: performance is competitive with prior tensor-based supervised methods on the Gutiérrez et al. (2016) dataset; method is effectively zero-shot because it requires only single-word vectors; larger windows and joint subspaces improve results; noun norm (BO) is the strongest single predictor; geometric patterns suggest metaphor is a contextual spectrum. The paper's reasoning chain connects (1) distributional co-occurrence capturing salient associations → (2) context-specific subspace selection reflecting joint semantics → (3) simple geometric summaries capturing degree of alignment/divergence between constituents → (4) logistic regression mapping geometry to metaphoricity. Strengths: clear end-to-end mapping from base space to interpretable features, thorough parametric grid (k, windows, selection types), and qualitative geometric analysis. Weaknesses in argument continuity appear around comparisons to prior work (incomplete comparability of V2), statistical-test reporting (missing test details), and the operationalisation of 'zero-shot' (training on dyads, no held-out-word split). Several assumptions (PMI choices, vocab cutoff, sufficiency of triangle features, CV strategy) are crucial but under-explored. Recommended next steps to strengthen causal claims: explicit leave-adjective/noun-out evaluations, report regression coefficients with CIs, and provide full statistical-test details and code/data to reproduce subspace selection indices.
logical_argument_graph: Node A: Distributional semantics (PMI base space from Wikipedia) is an adequate repository of word associations for metaphoricity detection.
Node B: For any adjective-noun pair, selecting salient PMI dimensions (subspace selection heuristics) yields a context-specific low-dimensional semantic subspace.
Edge A->B: The PMI base vectors provide the dimensions to select; assumptions: smoothing a=10k, vocab top-200k.
Node C: Geometric relationships (triangle side lengths, norms, normalized points) within the subspace capture the degree of correspondence/divergence between adjective and noun.
Edge B->C: Subspace selection transforms raw co-occurrence patterns into geometry amenable to simple summarisation.
Node D: Logistic regression mapping geometric features -> metaphoric vs literal label yields competitive classification performance.
Edge C->D: Empirical results (Table 1) show F-scores across parameter grid; BO (noun norm) singled out as strongest predictor (Table 3 references).
Node E: Larger context windows and joint/combined subspaces enhance semantic (syntagmatic) signal and improve classification.
Edge A->E: Argues via Sahlgren (2008) that wider windows shift from syntactic to semantic signal; Table 1 supports higher F-scores for 5+5.
Node F: Because features derive from individual word vectors (no phrase vectors), the method is effectively zero-shot and can handle unseen adjective-noun pairs.
Edge D->F (weakened): The model trains on dyads (labels) but claims zero-shot based on feature construction only; missing demonstration with held-out words weakens this edge.
Node G: Geometric patterns (e.g., horseshoe-like AB vs origin behaviour) suggest metaphoricity is a contextual spectrum rather than a strict binary mapping.
Edge C->G: Visualization and averaged ratios (Table 4) offered as evidence; interpretation partly qualitative and dataset-specific.

Breakpoints flagged: (i) A->B depends on PMI preprocessing and vocab choices; (ii) C->D relies on sufficiency of triangle features and linear classifier; (iii) D->F lacks experimental leave-word-out validation; (iv) comparisons to Gutiérrez et al. V2 are not strictly commensurable due to dataset subset uncertainty.

strengths.title: Clear mapping from theoretical premise to operational method
strengths.description: The paper coherently connects contextualist linguistic theory to a concrete algorithm: PMI base space → per-pair subspace selection → geometric summarisation → logistic regression.
evidence: Sections 2 and 3 articulate the theoretical motivation and outline the three desiderata for contextual, geometrically interpretable spaces.
Method section specifies PMI construction, five subspace heuristics, and triangle geometry features.

strengths.title: Systematic parametric exploration
strengths.description: The experiments evaluate multiple subspace selection heuristics, subspace dimensionalities (20,50,200,500) and two window sizes, showing consistent patterns across the grid.

Section 5 discusses trends (zipped best up to 200 dims; joint/independent improve at 500).

strengths.title: Interpretable features and qualitative analysis
strengths.description: Using simple geometric summaries (norms, pairwise lengths) aids interpretability and enables visualization/phenomenological analysis of metaphoricity as a spectrum.
evidence: Figure 2 visualises three example phrases across the spectrum while Section 5 interprets AB/BO/AO behaviours.
Authors perform single-feature regressions and discuss BO dominance.

concerns.description: The paper compares F-scores to Gutiérrez et al. V1/V2 but V2 results were obtained on an undisclosed reduced subset; the statistical comparison (χ2) lacks details. This undermines the strength of the cross-paper performance claim.

concerns.description: Although the feature construction uses single-word vectors, the classifier is trained on labelled dyads. There is no held-out-adjective or -noun experiment to demonstrate true zero-shot generalisation to unseen lexical items.

No indication of multiple seed runs for CV; random-seed sensitivity unreported.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide full logistic regression tables (coefficients, SEs, p-values, CIs) for single- and multi-feature models and report performance mean ± std over several CV random seeds.

concerns.description: The choice to summarise subspace geometry entirely by triangle side lengths (and a few normalized constructs) may omit important signals (angles, higher-order patterns) and could bias conclusions about which geometric properties matter.

Section 5 notes relatively poor predictiveness of some triangle-derived features (ADE).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Test alternative geometric summaries (cosine angles, pairwise cosines, principal component dispersion, higher-order moments) and report whether BO dominance persists.

concerns.description: PMI smoothing (a=10,000), vocab cutoff (top 200k), and +1 weighting choices materially affect the base space and hence subspace selection; sensitivity analyses are not provided.
evidence: Section 3 defines PMI with smoothing a=10,000 and +1; shared analysis flags A1, A6, A7 as critical assumptions.
Chaining notes recommend varying smoothing, vocabulary size and comparing to dense embeddings, but experiments do not report these.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide ablations varying smoothing constant a, vocabulary size, and compare to SVD-PPMI or word2vec representations to show robustness of the geometric phenomena.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a contextual geometric method for identifying metaphoric vs literal adjective-noun usages by dynamically selecting a k-dimensional PMI-based subspace per word pair and summarising geometry via triangle side lengths (norms/distances). These features feed a logistic regression classifier evaluated on the Gutiérrez et al. (2016) dataset under shuffled 10-fold cross-validation and compared to baselines (majority, word2vec cosine) and reported scores from the prior tensor-based method (Gutiérrez V1/V2). Main empirical findings: performance comparable to V1 and better than reported V2; performance improves with larger co-occurrence windows (5+5) and with joint/zippered subspace selection that uses both constituents; noun norm (BO) is the single most predictive feature. The paper also offers qualitative/visual analyses arguing that metaphoricity corresponds to systematic geometric changes, motivating an interpretation of metaphor as a contextually emergent spectrum. The core claims rest on (i) reproducible construction of PMI base space, (ii) faithful implementation of five subspace-selection heuristics, (iii) use of triangle-derived features, and (iv) logistic regression with CV. Key reproducibility and validity gaps include incomplete reporting of preprocessing details (tokenisation, punctuation, multiword handling), missing exact CV seeds/folds, insufficient statistical-test detail, no held-out leave-one-adjective/noun-out evaluation to validate zero-shot generalisation, and limited sensitivity analysis to PMI smoothing, vocabulary cutoffs, and alternative embedding bases.

Parameter choices (window size, k) modulate base cooccurrence counts -> affect chosen dims -> change geometry -> change classifier performance
Observed high BO predictive power + dataset adjective selection bias -> potential confound where adjective priors or noun frequency drive results
Comparison to Gutiérrez et al. V2 based on reported numbers (reduced subset) -> ambiguous direct comparability -> interpretation that method is competitive but not definitively superior

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that metaphoricity of adjective-noun pairs can be detected by constructing, per input pair, an ad-hoc lower-dimensional subspace of a large PMI-based distributional base space and then summarising the relative geometry of the adjective and noun within that subspace via simple triangle-derived features (vector norms and pairwise distances). The method selects subspace dimensions using PMI salience according to several heuristics (Joint, Independent, Zipped, Adjective-Only, Noun-Only), computes geometric features for two aligned triangles (ABO and CDE), and uses a standardised logistic regression to predict binary metaphoric vs literal labels. Empirically, on the Gutiérrez et al. (2016) dataset, the model obtains F-scores close to or exceeding the relevant variant (V2) of that prior tensor-based method; larger context windows (5+5) and subspaces that combine information from both constituents tend to improve performance; the noun vector norm (BO) is reported as the single most predictive feature. The authors interpret systematic variation in geometric features as supporting a continuous, contextually emergent view of metaphor rather than a strict categorical mapping. The paper leans on prior work (McGregor et al. 2015; Agres et al. 2016) for the contextualised-subspace idea but extends it to metaphoricity detection, emphasises interpretability and zero-shot applicability (no phrase vectors required), and provides parameter studies (window size, k) and qualitative visualisations. Key methodological dependencies and risks include reliance on PMI from a Wikipedia dump, choices for PMI smoothing/vocabulary cutoffs, the 10-fold shuffled CV evaluation (no leave-one-adjective/noun-out reported), and limited disclosure of certain statistics (detailed p-values, regression coefficients, and the reduced subset used by Gutiérrez et al.).
logical_argument_graph: L1: Metaphor is contextually emergent and can be modelled by ad-hoc, context-specific semantic subspaces (theoretical premise referencing McGregor et al., Wilson & Sperber, Carston).
L2: Build a large PMI-based base space from a large corpus (Wikipedia); PMI dimensions encode salient lexical associations (operational assumption A1).
L3: For each adjective-noun pair, select a k-dimensional subspace by heuristics (Joint/Independent/Zipped/Adj/Noun) based on PMI salience (assumption A2).
L4: Project adjective and noun word-vectors into this subspace and compute geometric summaries (triangle sides/norms etc.; assumption A3).
L5: Train a logistic regression on these geometric features to predict metaphoricity (assumption A4), evaluate by shuffled 10-fold CV on Gutiérrez et al. data (assumption A5, A8).
L6: Empirical observation: larger windows and joint-type subspaces improve F-scores; noun-norm (BO) is most predictive (empirical claims C4, C5).
L7: Comparative observation: performance comparable to Gutiérrez et al. V1 and exceeding their V2 as reported (claim C1) with caveats about dataset subset and test details.
L8: Interpretive claim: geometry patterns across examples indicate a continuum/spectrum of metaphoricity; visual and aggregated statistics support spectrum view (claim C3).
L9: Consequence: the method is effectively zero-shot (no phrase vectors required) enabling application to unseen adjective-noun pairs, subject to vocabulary coverage of PMI base (claim C2).

strengths.title: Context-sensitive subspace construction

strengths.description: The method avoids phrase-level vectors, enabling application to arbitrary in-vocabulary word pairs without needing phrase observations.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either (a) obtain or reconstruct the same reduced subset to rerun evaluations for exact comparability, or (b) report comparisons only against V1 on the same full set and clearly caveat V2 comparisons; include confidence intervals and exact p-values for significance claims.

Zero-shot is described operationally but not validated on held-out-vocabulary splits.

concerns.title: Insufficient statistical reporting
concerns.description: Statistical claims (e.g., 'significant at p<0.05 using χ2') lack test statistics, contingency tables, degrees of freedom, and exact p-values; single-feature regressions and coefficient uncertainties are not fully reported.

concerns.description: Triangle-side lengths are plausible but may omit other geometric signals (angles, higher-order interactions, distributional mass); assumption that these summaries are sufficient is not fully validated.

The spectrum claim is couched in theoretical rhetoric referencing pragmatics and ad-hoc concepts.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either obtain graded metaphoricity judgements for a sample and compute correlations with geometric scores, or clarify that the 'spectrum' claim is exploratory and derived from model rankings rather than independent graded evidence.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a contextually dynamic, geometric method for metaphor identification: build a large PMI-based base matrix from Wikipedia, then for each adjective-noun candidate select an ad-hoc k-dimensional subspace (five selection heuristics) based on salient PMI dimensions of the constituent words, compute geometric summaries (triangle side lengths and norms), and use those as features in a logistic-regression classifier to predict metaphoric vs literal usage. The method is argued to be effectively zero-shot because it uses only individual-word statistics rather than phrase vectors. Empirically, the model is evaluated on the Gutiérrez et al. (2016) adjective-noun dataset across choices of k and co-occurrence window, reporting F-scores comparable to or exceeding the more general variant (V2) of Gutiérrez et al. The authors interpret patterns in the geometry (e.g., noun norm BO dominance, AB/centroid relationships) as evidence that metaphoricity is a contextually emergent spectrum that can be read off interpretable geometric features. The chain of inference is: (1) PMI captures salient lexical associations; (2) selecting context-relevant PMI dimensions creates meaningful ad-hoc subspaces; (3) geometric relations in these subspaces summarize conceptual alignment/divergence between constituents; (4) those summaries correlate with metaphoricity and can generalise to unseen phrases because they use only single-word information.
logical_argument_graph: A1: PMI-based vectors (Wikipedia) encode salient lexical associations relevant to composition.
A2: For any word-pair {a,n}, selecting top-k PMI dimensions tied to a and/or n yields a contextual subspace that foregrounds relevant associations.
A3: Geometry in that subspace (norms, pairwise distances, triangles) summarises alignment or divergence between the constituents' associations.
A4: Divergence/widening or shifts relative to the origin correlate with metaphoricity (more divergence/particular patterns → more metaphoric).
A5: Extracting simple geometric features (triangle sides) and using logistic regression is sufficient to detect these correlations.
A6: Because only single-word statistics are used, the method can be applied to adjective-noun pairs unseen as phrases (zero-shot).

A7: Empirically, on the Gutiérrez et al. dataset, the method achieves F-scores comparable to or better than the non-phrase/tensor baseline (V2), and parameter sweeps (k, window, selection method) reveal interpretable trends (joint/zipped vs independent, larger windows help).
A8: Therefore, metaphor can be modelled as a context-sensitive geometric phenomenon emergent in ad-hoc subspaces; the method is simple, interpretable, and practically useful for unseen phrases.
